newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Arab neighbours shun Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Arab neighbours shun Netanyahu.

text.p: Israel's Arab friends were slamming the door in the face of right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli media said on Sunday.
"Arab leaders boycott Netanyahu until the evacuation of Hebron," screamed the red headline topping Israel's biggest newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
Foreign Ministry Director-General Eytan Bentsur acknowledged problems, saying Israel was doing all it could to fix relations.
The problems with peace partners Egypt, Jordan and the Palestinians emerged over the long-delayed Israeli pullback from the West Bank city of Hebron agreed more than a year ago.
"We're taking a series of initiatives and actions and I believe that in a not-too-distant time we will see that things are improving," Bentsur told Israel Radio without elaborating.
Arab leaders made a point of inviting two other prominent Israelis -- Labour head Shimon Peres, ousted by Netanyahu as prime minister in May, and President Ezer Weizman.
Peres was summoned to Nablus in the West Bank by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Sunday and to Egypt by President Hosni Mubarak next week, a spokeswoman for Peres said.
Weizman, whose job is largely ceremonial, was due on Monday in Egypt where he is seen as an elder statesman in contrast with the young and less experienced Netanyahu.
Mubarak said on Saturday that he refused to meet Netanyahu until Israel solved the Hebron issue with the Palestinians.
"The situation is still complicated. There's no (Israeli) commitment to what was agreed," Mubarak told reporters.
Israel Radio said Netanyahu's political adviser Dore Gold would meet Jordan's ambassador to try to arrange a higher-level meeting that in the past would have been no problem.
The Hebron redeployment should have been carried out in March but was delayed by Peres after Islamic militant suicide bombers killed 59 people in Israel in February and March.
It was frozen by Netanyahu, who says changes are needed to the deal to ensure the security of 400 Jewish settlers living in enclaves amidst 100,000 Arabs in Hebron.
But the Palestinians refuse to amend the Hebron accord.
Egyptian newspapers, many of them state institutions, have described Netanyahu as stupid, arrogant and deceitful.
On Saturday an official Syrian newspaper accused Netanyahu of trying to start war in the Middle East and urged Arab countries to unite in preparation.
"Such a foolish man is crazy enough to take an important decision that could explode and destroy the region," Ameed al-Khouli, director general of al-Thawra newspaper, wrote.
In Israel, local media reported that 33 Israeli reserve soldiers had written an open letter to Netanyahu warning him against involving the Jewish state in a war.
Israel, which had tightened an entry ban against Palestinians after clashes last month triggered by Netanyahu's policies in Jerusalem, began easing restrictions on Sunday.
But Palestinian officials said only 3,000 left for work pending issuance of all 35,000 promised entry permits.
U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross, mediating in talks between Israel and the Palestinians on implementing the Hebron troop redeployment, met Arafat in Nablus on Saturday.
"Obviously there are differences and we're trying to find the best way to overcome them," Ross told reporters afterwards.

Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said there was "not one inch of progress" in the Israeli-Palestinian talks due to resume on Monday in Taba, Egypt. He urged Washington to push Israel to keep the deal reached by its previous government.
